claim: Vibrio alginolyticus VemP controls the expression of SecD/F that stimulates a late step of translocation by undergoing export-regulated elongation arrest.
source: Vibrio alginolyticus VemP controls the expression of SecD/F that stimulates a late step of translocation by undergoing export-regulated elongation arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding from previous work, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The signal recognition particle (SRP) interacts with VemP nascent chain.
source: we attempted at delineating the pathway of the VemP nascent-chain interaction with Sec-related factors, and identified the signal recognition particle (SRP) and PpiD (a membrane-anchored periplasmic chaperone) in addition to other translocon components and a ribosomal protein as interacting partners.
evidence: Identified through systematic photo-crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 1E and supported by functional studies in Figure 3.

claim: PpiD (a membrane-anchored periplasmic chaperone) interacts with VemP nascent chain.
source: we attempted at delineating the pathway of the VemP nascent-chain interaction with Sec-related factors, and identified the signal recognition particle (SRP) and PpiD (a membrane-anchored periplasmic chaperone) in addition to other translocon components and a ribosomal protein as interacting partners.
evidence: Identified through systematic photo-crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 1F and supported by functional studies in Figure 4.

claim: SRP is required for the membrane-targeting of VemP.
source: Our results showed that SRP is required for the membrane-targeting of VemP, whereas PpiD acts cooperatively with SecD/F in the translocation and arrest-cancelation of VemP.
evidence: Demonstrated by Ffh-depletion experiments in Figure 3A showing stabilization of the AP-un form of VemP.

claim: PpiD acts cooperatively with SecD/F in the translocation and arrest-cancelation of VemP.
source: Our results showed that SRP is required for the membrane-targeting of VemP, whereas PpiD acts cooperatively with SecD/F in the translocation and arrest-cancelation of VemP.
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic complementation experiments in Figure 4D showing that overproduction of either PpiD or SecD/F alone cannot rescue the defect caused by loss of the other.

claim: The conserved Arg-85 residue of VemP is a crucial element that confers PpiD-dependence to VemP.
source: We also identified the conserved Arg-85 residue of VemP as a crucial element that confers PpiD-dependence to VemP and plays an essential role in the regulated arrest-cancelation.
evidence: Demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments in Figure 5 showing that R85W mutation reduces PpiD-dependency of VemP translocation.

claim: Arg-85 plays an essential role in the regulated arrest-cancelation of VemP.
source: We also identified the conserved Arg-85 residue of VemP as a crucial element that confers PpiD-dependence to VemP and plays an essential role in the regulated arrest-cancelation.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments in Figure 5A showing that mutations at Arg-85 destabilize the translation arrest of VemP.

claim: VemP monitors late steps in the protein translocation pathway.
source: We propose a scheme of the arrest-cancelation processes of VemP, which likely monitors late steps in the protein translocation pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that VemP arrest-cancelation depends on SecD/F and PpiD, which function at late steps of translocation, and that the majority of arrested VemP has its signal sequence processed.

claim: The Sec translocon consists of three membrane-integrated proteins, SecY, SecE, and SecG.
source: The translocon consists of three membrane-integrated proteins, SecY, SecE, and SecG (Mori and Ito, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to Mori and Ito, 2001.

claim: SecY forms a channel-like path for substrate secretory proteins.
source: SecY forms a channel-like path for substrate secretory proteins (Van den Berg et al., 2004) and is stabilized by SecE (Taura et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Van den Berg et al., 2004.

claim: SecY is stabilized by SecE.
source: SecY forms a channel-like path for substrate secretory proteins (Van den Berg et al., 2004) and is stabilized by SecE (Taura et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Taura et al., 1993.

claim: SecG peripherally binds to SecY.
source: SecG peripherally binds to SecY (Tanaka et al., 2015) and stimulates the SecA-dependent protein translocation (Nishiyama et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 2015.

claim: SecG stimulates the SecA-dependent protein translocation.
source: SecG peripherally binds to SecY (Tanaka et al., 2015) and stimulates the SecA-dependent protein translocation (Nishiyama et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Nishiyama et al., 1994.

claim: SecA is an essential ATPase.
source: SecA, an essential ATPase (Lill et al., 1989), binds to cytoplasmic protrusions in SecY (Mori and Ito, 2006a; Zimmer et al., 2008) and pushes a polypeptide into the translocon (Economou and Wickner, 1994; Erlandson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Lill et al., 1989.

claim: SecA binds to cytoplasmic protrusions in SecY.
source: SecA, an essential ATPase (Lill et al., 1989), binds to cytoplasmic protrusions in SecY (Mori and Ito, 2006a; Zimmer et al., 2008) and pushes a polypeptide into the translocon (Economou and Wickner, 1994; Erlandson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Mori and Ito, 2006a and Zimmer et al., 2008.

claim: SecA pushes a polypeptide into the translocon.
source: SecA, an essential ATPase (Lill et al., 1989), binds to cytoplasmic protrusions in SecY (Mori and Ito, 2006a; Zimmer et al., 2008) and pushes a polypeptide into the translocon (Economou and Wickner, 1994; Erlandson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Economou and Wickner, 1994 and Erlandson et al., 2008.

claim: Some secretory proteins use the signal recognition particle (SRP) pathway, which targets the nascent precursor protein to the translocon.
source: Although bacterial protein secretion to the periplasmic space is thought to occur post-translationally in many cases, some secretory proteins use the signal recognition particle (SRP) pathway, which targets the nascent precursor protein to the translocon (Huber et al., 2005; Shimohata et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Huber et al., 2005 and Shimohata et al., 2005.

claim: Even in cases where proteins use the SRP pathway, translocation requires the SecA motor function.
source: Notably, even in the latter cases, translocation requires the SecA motor function (Shimohata et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Shimohata et al., 2005.

claim: SRP binds to the signal sequence equivalent (a TM segment) of a membrane protein and delivers a ribosome-nascent protein complex (RNC) to the translocon.
source: SRP binds to the signal sequence equivalent (a TM segment) of a membrane protein and deliverers a ribosome-nascent protein complex (RNC) to the translocon (Steinberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Steinberg et al., 2018.

claim: The RNC binds to the same SecY region as SecA.
source: The RNC binds to the same SecY region as SecA (Frauenfeld et al., 2011; Kuhn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Frauenfeld et al., 2011 and Kuhn et al., 2011.

claim: The SecD/F complex stimulates protein secretion in vivo.
source: Bacteria also have the SecD/F complex that stimulates protein secretion in vivo (Pogliano and Beckwith, 1994) and facilitates the release of a polypeptide from the Sec translocon during a late step in translocation (Matsuyama et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Pogliano and Beckwith, 1994.

claim: SecD/F facilitates the release of a polypeptide from the Sec translocon during a late step in translocation.
source: Bacteria also have the SecD/F complex that stimulates protein secretion in vivo (Pogliano and Beckwith, 1994) and facilitates the release of a polypeptide from the Sec translocon during a late step in translocation (Matsuyama et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Matsuyama et al., 1993.

claim: SecD/F is a H+-driven motor, in which its periplasmic domain (P1 head) binds a translocon-engaged substrate.
source: Structural and functional analyses have shown that SecD/F is a H+-driven motor, in which its periplasmic domain (P1 head) binds a translocon-engaged substrate (Furukawa et al., 2017) and undergoes a conformational change coupled with the H+ flow (Tsukazaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Furukawa et al., 2017 and Tsukazaki et al., 2011.

claim: The P1 head of SecD/F undergoes a conformational change coupled with the H+ flow.
source: Structural and functional analyses have shown that SecD/F is a H+-driven motor, in which its periplasmic domain (P1 head) binds a translocon-engaged substrate (Furukawa et al., 2017) and undergoes a conformational change coupled with the H+ flow (Tsukazaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tsukazaki et al., 2011.

claim: Vibrio alginolyticus possesses two sets of the secD/F genes, designated V.secD1/F1 and V.secD2/F2.
source: A marine bacterium, V. alginolyticus, possesses two sets of the secD/F genes, designated V.secD1/F1 and V.secD2/F2, whose products utilize Na+- and presumably H+-motive forces, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: V.SecD1/F1 utilizes Na+-motive force.
source: A marine bacterium, V. alginolyticus, possesses two sets of the secD/F genes, designated V.secD1/F1 and V.secD2/F2, whose products utilize Na+- and presumably H+-motive forces, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: V.SecD2/F2 presumably utilizes H+-motive force.
source: A marine bacterium, V. alginolyticus, possesses two sets of the secD/F genes, designated V.secD1/F1 and V.secD2/F2, whose products utilize Na+- and presumably H+-motive forces, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a presumption based on previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: V. alginolyticus adapts quickly to a salinity change by replacing SecD/F paralogues.
source: The bacterium adapts quickly to a salinity change by replacing these SecD/F paralogues (Ishii et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: V.secD1/F1 is expressed constitutively.
source: Although V.secD1/F1 is expressed constitutively, the expression of V.secD2/F2 is tightly repressed under Na+-rich growth conditions, but induced under low Na+ growth conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: The expression of V.secD2/F2 is tightly repressed under Na+-rich growth conditions.
source: Although V.secD1/F1 is expressed constitutively, the expression of V.secD2/F2 is tightly repressed under Na+-rich growth conditions, but induced under low Na+ growth conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: The expression of V.secD2/F2 is induced under low Na+ growth conditions.
source: Although V.secD1/F1 is expressed constitutively, the expression of V.secD2/F2 is tightly repressed under Na+-rich growth conditions, but induced under low Na+ growth conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: The vemP gene is located upstream of V.secD2/F2 on the same operon.
source: The vemP gene located upstream of V.secD2/F2 on the same operon plays an essential role in the regulated expression of V.secD2/F2.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: VemP plays an essential role in the regulated expression of V.secD2/F2.
source: The vemP gene located upstream of V.secD2/F2 on the same operon plays an essential role in the regulated expression of V.secD2/F2.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: VemP undergoes stable translation-arrest before the canonical termination step under a protein translocation-deficient condition.
source: It undergoes stable translation-arrest before the canonical termination step under a protein translocation-deficient condition.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: The stalled ribosome on a vemP-V.secD2/F2 mRNA destabilizes a stem-loop structure in the vemP-V.secD2 intergenic region, leading to the exposure of an otherwise masked ribosome-binding site for the V.secD2 gene.
source: In this scenario, the stalled ribosome on a vemP-V.secD2/F2 mRNA destabilizes a stem-loop structure in the vemP-V.secD2 intergenic region, leading to the exposure of an otherwise masked ribosome-binding site for the V.secD2 gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: The VemP translation-arrest occurs even under a protein translocation competent condition.
source: Importantly, the VemP translation-arrest occurs even under a protein translocation competent condition, but it is rapidly canceled presumably by a translocation-coupled pulling force that drives translocation of VemP.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: The VemP translation-arrest is rapidly canceled presumably by a translocation-coupled pulling force that drives translocation of VemP.
source: Importantly, the VemP translation-arrest occurs even under a protein translocation competent condition, but it is rapidly canceled presumably by a translocation-coupled pulling force that drives translocation of VemP.
evidence: This is a presumption based on previous observations, supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: The majority of VemP has its signal sequence processed even in the arrested state.
source: Our previous in vivo studies showed that the majority of VemP has its signal sequence processed even in the arrested state.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation to Mori et al., 2018.

claim: The arrest-cancelation of VemP occurs after its translocation has proceeded beyond the signal sequence processing event on the Sec translocon.
source: This strongly suggests that the arrest-cancelation of VemP occurs after its translocation has proceeded beyond the signal sequence processing event on the Sec translocon (Mori et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the majority of arrested VemP has its signal sequence processed, supported by citation to Mori et al., 2018.

claim: Site-directed in vivo photo-crosslinking is a well-designed technique for analysis of inter- or intra-molecular interactions of proteins in living cells.
source: Site-directed in vivo photo-crosslinking is a well-designed technique for analysis of inter- or intra-molecular interactions of proteins in living cells (Chin and Schultz, 2002), wherein a pair of a mutated tRNA and an engineered tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase allows for in vivo incorporation of a photo-reactive amino acid analog, p-benzoyl-L-phenylalanine (pBPA), into any selected positions of a target protein by amber suppression (Chin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Chin and Schultz, 2002 and Chin et al., 2002.

claim: A pair of a mutated tRNA and an engineered tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase allows for in vivo incorporation of pBPA into any selected positions of a target protein by amber suppression.
source: Site-directed in vivo photo-crosslinking is a well-designed technique for analysis of inter- or intra-molecular interactions of proteins in living cells (Chin and Schultz, 2002), wherein a pair of a mutated tRNA and an engineered tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase allows for in vivo incorporation of a photo-reactive amino acid analog, p-benzoyl-L-phenylalanine (pBPA), into any selected positions of a target protein by amber suppression (Chin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Chin et al., 2002.

claim: The PiXie method allows precisely time-controlled and residue-specific crosslinking.
source: We previously used the PiXie method, which allows precisely time-controlled and residue-specific crosslinking, to analyze the post-translational maturation processes of protein complexes with different cellular localizations in bacteria (Miyazaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation to Miyazaki et al., 2018.

claim: Vibrio species are closely related to enterobacteria including E. coli.
source: Vibrio species are closely related to enterobacteria including E. coli and possess a single copy of the secA, secY, secE, secG, and ffh (encoding the protein component of SRP) genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Vibrio species possess a single copy of the secA, secY, secE, secG, and ffh genes.
source: Vibrio species are closely related to enterobacteria including E. coli and possess a single copy of the secA, secY, secE, secG, and ffh (encoding the protein component of SRP) genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The SecA homolog of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells.
source: Because each of the SecA (Kunioka et al., 1998), SecY (Bhattacharyya and Das, 1997), SecE (Nishiyama et al., 1998) and the two SecD/F (Ishii et al., 2015) homologs of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells, the basic structure and function of the Sec machinery and the interaction modes among these factors should be well conserved between these species.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Kunioka et al., 1998.

claim: The SecY homolog of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells.
source: Because each of the SecA (Kunioka et al., 1998), SecY (Bhattacharyya and Das, 1997), SecE (Nishiyama et al., 1998) and the two SecD/F (Ishii et al., 2015) homologs of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells, the basic structure and function of the Sec machinery and the interaction modes among these factors should be well conserved between these species.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Bhattacharyya and Das, 1997.

claim: The SecE homolog of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells.
source: Because each of the SecA (Kunioka et al., 1998), SecY (Bhattacharyya and Das, 1997), SecE (Nishiyama et al., 1998) and the two SecD/F (Ishii et al., 2015) homologs of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells, the basic structure and function of the Sec machinery and the interaction modes among these factors should be well conserved between these species.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Nishiyama et al., 1998.

claim: The two SecD/F homologs of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells.
source: Because each of the SecA (Kunioka et al., 1998), SecY (Bhattacharyya and Das, 1997), SecE (Nishiyama et al., 1998) and the two SecD/F (Ishii et al., 2015) homologs of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells, the basic structure and function of the Sec machinery and the interaction modes among these factors should be well conserved between these species.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2015.

claim: The basic structure and function of the Sec machinery and the interaction modes among these factors should be well conserved between Vibrio and E. coli.
source: Because each of the SecA (Kunioka et al., 1998), SecY (Bhattacharyya and Das, 1997), SecE (Nishiyama et al., 1998) and the two SecD/F (Ishii et al., 2015) homologs of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells, the basic structure and function of the Sec machinery and the interaction modes among these factors should be well conserved between these species.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional complementation of Vibrio Sec components in E. coli.

claim: VemP(W124pBPA) generates a crosslink of ~30 kDa that is immunoprecipitable with an anti-uL22 antibody.
source: An XL of ~30 kDa, observed for the VemP(W124pBPA) variant, was immunoprecipitatable with an anti-uL22 antibody (Figure 1B, right).
evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking and immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Trp-124 of VemP is positioned close to the ribosomal protein uL22 in vivo.
source: The proximity of Trp-124 to uL22 in vivo is consistent with a recent cryo-EM study showing that Trp-124 of arrested VemP is positioned close to the ribosomal protein uL22 (Figure 1B, left) (Su et al., 2017).
evidence: The in vivo crosslinking data is consistent with the cryo-EM structure, supported by citation to Su et al., 2017.

claim: VemP(F81pBPA) and VemP(T83pBPA) generate crosslinks of ~25 kDa that contain SecG.
source: VemP(F81pBPA) and VemP(T83pBPA) generated XLs of ~25 kDa. We envisioned that the crosslinked partner could either be SecE (~14 kDa) or SecG (~12 kDa), small components of the translocon, because VemP engages in the Sec-dependent translocation (Mori et al., 2018). We reasoned that these XLs contained SecG because they reacted with an anti-SecG antibody (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and disappeared in the ΔsecG strain (VemP(F81pBPA); Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking, immunoprecipitation, and genetic experiments shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: VemP derivatives having pBPA in a middle region (Arg-74, Asp-76, Leu-78, Asn-82, and Trp-86) generate crosslinks with SecY.
source: To investigate possible crosslinking with SecY, the main component of the translocon, we used a host strain having a chromosomal secY-his10 gene. We detected the SecYxVemP XLs for the VemP derivatives having pBPA in a middle region (Arg-74, Asp-76, Leu-78, Asn-82, and Trp-86) of VemP among materials pulled-down by polyhistidine affinity isolation (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking and His-tag affinity purification experiments shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: VemP interacts with Ffh through its signal sequence (Ala-15 position).
source: We found that VemP also interacts with SRP through the PiXie analysis using a strain carrying chromosomal ffh-his10. Placement of pBPA within the signal sequence (Ala-15 position) allowed for the generation of a VemPxFfh XL that was His-tag affinity isolated (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking and His-tag affinity purification experiments shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: PpiD interacts with the VemP region (Tyr-36 to Ser-60) that follows the periplasmic end of the signal sequence.
source: We addressed the possibility of their involvement using their His-tagged derivatives and found that a XL was His-tag affinity-isolated when a cell with chromosomal ppiD-his10 was used (Figure 1F), but not with the other his10 constructs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,D). Furthermore, the XL was immunoprecipitated with an anti-PpiD antibody and were not generated in a ΔppiD cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B). These results indicate that PpiD interacts with the VemP region (Tyr-36 to Ser-60) that follows the periplasmic end of the signal sequence.
evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking, His-tag affinity purification, immunoprecipitation, and genetic experiments shown in Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,D.

claim: None of the VemP crosslinks with uL22, Ffh, SecG, SecY, and PpiD were immunoprecipitated with the anti-FLAG antibody, indicating that the VemP component in these crosslinks lacks the C-terminal tag and are in the elongation-arrested state.
source: None of the VemP XLs with uL22, Ffh, SecG, SecY, and PpiD described above were immunoprecipitated with the anti-FLAG antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), indicating that the VemP component in these XLs lacks the C-terminal tag and, therefore, are in the elongation-arrested state.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The uL22- and Ffh-crosslinks decreased slightly faster than the arrested VemP during the chase period.
source: While the decrease rates of the SecG-XLs and the arrested VemP were almost the same, the uL22- and Ffh-XLs decreased slightly faster than the arrested VemP (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by kinetic analysis of crosslinks during pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The decrease rates of the SecG-crosslinks and the arrested VemP were almost the same.
source: While the decrease rates of the SecG-XLs and the arrested VemP were almost the same, the uL22- and Ffh-XLs decreased slightly faster than the arrested VemP (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by kinetic analysis of crosslinks during pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ffh (SRP) and uL22 interact with the arrested VemP polypeptide before targeting to the translocon.
source: These results suggest that Ffh (SRP) and uL22 interact with the arrested VemP polypeptide before targeting to the translocon, in agreement with their cellular functions and localization.
evidence: Inferred from the kinetic analysis showing that uL22- and Ffh-crosslinks decrease faster than arrested VemP, and consistent with their known cellular functions.

claim: NaN3 treatment of cells causes the stabilization of the AP-un form of VemP in living cells.
source: This was verified by examining the effect of NaN3, a SecA inhibitor, on the VemP-crosslinkings. NaN3 treatment of cells causes the stabilization of the AP-un form of VemP in living cells (Mori et al., 2018), suggesting that inhibition of SecA prevents VemP from initiating its translocation into the translocon.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation to Mori et al., 2018.

claim: Inhibition of SecA prevents VemP from initiating its translocation into the translocon.
source: NaN3 treatment of cells causes the stabilization of the AP-un form of VemP in living cells (Mori et al., 2018), suggesting that inhibition of SecA prevents VemP from initiating its translocation into the translocon. We confirmed it by pulse-chase experiments using a secA51 (Ts) mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inferred from the stabilization of AP-un form upon NaN3 treatment and confirmed by experiments with secA51(Ts) mutant shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The arrest cancelation of VemP was severely and specifically retarded at high temperature in the secA51(Ts) mutant cells.
source: We confirmed it by pulse-chase experiments using a secA51 (Ts) mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). As expected, the arrest cancelation of VemP was severely and specifically retarded at high temperature in the secA51(Ts) mutant cells, but not in its isogenic wild type cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: NaN3 treatment increased the VemP crosslinking with uL22 and Ffh.
source: We found that the NaN3 treatment increased the VemP crosslinking with uL22 and Ffh, but decreased its crosslinking with SecY, SecG, and PpiD (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking experiments with NaN3 treatment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: NaN3 treatment decreased VemP crosslinking with SecY, SecG, and PpiD.
source: We found that the NaN3 treatment increased the VemP crosslinking with uL22 and Ffh, but decreased its crosslinking with SecY, SecG, and PpiD (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking experiments with NaN3 treatment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B.

claim: The arrested VemP interacts with SRP and uL22 before the interactions with the translocon and PpiD on the membrane.
source: These results suggest that the arrested VemP interacts with SRP and uL22 before the interactions with the translocon and PpiD on the membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the NaN3 treatment experiments showing increased crosslinking with uL22 and Ffh but decreased crosslinking with SecY, SecG, and PpiD.

claim: The PpiD-crosslinks tended to decrease more slowly than SecG-crosslinks or the arrested VemP.
source: In contrast to the uL22- and Ffh-XLs, the PpiD-XLs tended to decrease more slowly than SecG-XLs or the arrested VemP (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by kinetic analysis of crosslinks during pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: VemP is recognized by PpiD after it engages with the translocon.
source: This suggests that VemP is recognized by PpiD after it engages with the translocon, being consistent with the topology of PpiD that has a functional domain in the periplasm.
evidence: Inferred from the kinetic analysis showing that PpiD-crosslinks decrease more slowly than SecG-crosslinks, and consistent with the known topology of PpiD.

claim: The Ffh-depletion upon removal of arabinose from the medium stabilized the AP-un form of VemP.
source: The Ffh-depletion upon removal of arabinose from the medium stabilized the AP-un form of VemP (Figure 3A), indicating an impairment of the targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments using Ffh-depletable strain shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ffh-depletion impairs the targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon.
source: The Ffh-depletion upon removal of arabinose from the medium stabilized the AP-un form of VemP (Figure 3A), indicating an impairment of the targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon.
evidence: Inferred from the stabilization of AP-un form upon Ffh-depletion shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Deletion of the secB gene severely compromised export of MBP, a SecB-dependent substrate.
source: Consistent with the observation, deletion of the secB gene that encodes a secretion-specific chaperone severely compromised export of MBP, a SecB-dependent substrate, but exhibited the normal arrest cancelation of VemP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting the co-translational targeting of a VemP-ribosome complex.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments using ΔsecB strain shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of the secB gene exhibited the normal arrest cancelation of VemP.
source: Consistent with the observation, deletion of the secB gene that encodes a secretion-specific chaperone severely compromised export of MBP, a SecB-dependent substrate, but exhibited the normal arrest cancelation of VemP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting the co-translational targeting of a VemP-ribosome complex.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments using ΔsecB strain shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The synthesis of V.SecD2 was elevated under the Ffh-depleted conditions in E. coli cells carrying a vemP-V.secD2/F2 plasmid.
source: To verify this point, we examined the V.SecD2 expression in WAM121 cells carrying a vemP-V.secD2/F2 plasmid, and found that the synthesis of V.SecD2 was indeed elevated under the Ffh-depleted conditions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the Ffh-depletable strain of V. alginolyticus, the V.SecD2 expression was induced in the arabinose-free medium even in the presence of a sufficient level of Na+.
source: We also examined the effect of an Ffh-depletion on the V.SecD2 expression in the cognate organism, V. alginolyticus (Figure 3C). Under a Na+-rich growth condition, the Na+-driven V.SecD1/F1 in this organism was fully functional, leading to the efficient arrest cancelation of VemP and consequent tight repression of V.SecD2 (Ishii et al., 2015). In the Ffh-depletable strain of V. alginolyticus with the arabinose promoter-controlled ffh, the V.SecD2 expression was induced in the arabinose-free medium even in the presence of a sufficient level of Na+, consistent with the notion that the Ffh-depletion compromises the targeting of VemP and stabilizes its translation arrest.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SRP is crucial for the translocon targeting of VemP, which is a prerequisite for the proper regulation of the V.SecD2/F2 expression in Vibrio.
source: These results suggest that SRP is crucial for the translocon targeting of VemP, which is a prerequisite for the proper regulation of the V.SecD2/F2 expression in Vibrio.
evidence: Inferred from the experiments showing that Ffh-depletion stabilizes VemP arrest and induces V.SecD2 expression in both E. coli and V. alginolyticus.

claim: VemP was kept in the arrested state much more stably in the ΔppiD cells than in the ppiD+ E. coli cells.
source: Pulse-chase analysis showed that VemP was kept in the arrested state much more stably in the ΔppiD cells than in the ppiD+ E. coli cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Translocation of MBP was retarded by the ppiD disruption, albeit less pronouncedly than VemP.
source: We note that translocation of a secretory protein MBP (maltose-binding protein) was also retarded by the ppiD disruption, albeit less pronouncedly (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The loss of ppiD increased the V.SecD2 expression in E. coli.
source: The loss of ppiD increased the V.SecD2 expression in E. coli (Figure 4B) and in Vibrio (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The loss of ppiD increased the V.SecD2 expression in Vibrio.
source: The loss of ppiD increased the V.SecD2 expression in E. coli (Figure 4B) and in Vibrio (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PpiD plays a crucial role in the arrest-cancelation of VemP.
source: These results show that PpiD plays a crucial role in the arrest-cancelation of VemP.
evidence: Inferred from the experiments showing that ppiD disruption stabilizes VemP arrest and induces V.SecD2 expression.

claim: The PpiD disruption caused an accumulation of the AP-pro form of VemP.
source: The PpiD disruption caused an accumulation of the AP-pro form of VemP in contrast to the Ffh depletion that led to the AP-un accumulation (compare Figures 3A and 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing pulse-chase experiments shown in Figures 3A and 4A.

claim: PpiD acts on the periplasmic side after the signal sequence cleavage of the arrested VemP.
source: These results support the notion that PpiD acts on the periplasmic side after the signal sequence cleavage of the arrested VemP, whereas Ffh acts earlier on the cytosolic side.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PpiD disruption causes accumulation of AP-pro form while Ffh depletion causes accumulation of AP-un form.

claim: Ffh acts earlier on the cytosolic side compared to PpiD.
source: These results support the notion that PpiD acts on the periplasmic side after the signal sequence cleavage of the arrested VemP, whereas Ffh acts earlier on the cytosolic side.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ffh depletion causes accumulation of AP-un form while PpiD disruption causes accumulation of AP-pro form.

claim: The overproduction of SecD/F facilitated the arrest cancelation in wild type cells.
source: The role of SecD/F itself in the VemP arrest cancelation can be seen from the prolonged VemP arrest in the secD1 (a mutation causing SecD/F depletion) E. coli cells (Figure 4D, vector lanes) and the enhanced arrest cancelation by overproduction of SecD/F (Figure 4D, left, vector vs. secD/F).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The arrested state of VemP was stabilized in the ΔppiD cells.
source: The arrested state of VemP was stabilized in the ΔppiD cells (Figure 4D, vector lanes), showing that its function is required for the active translocation and the arrest cancelation of VemP.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The overproduction of PpiD facilitated the arrest cancelation in wild type cells.
source: Whereas the overproduction of PpiD facilitated the arrest cancelation, as expected, SecD/F's overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the ppiD defect.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SecD/F's overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the ppiD defect.
source: Whereas the overproduction of PpiD facilitated the arrest cancelation, as expected, SecD/F's overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the ppiD defect.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PpiD overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the secD1 mutation.
source: Conversely, PpiD overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the secD1 mutation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Both SecD/F and PpiD are specifically required for the cancelation of VemP arrest.
source: These results rule out the possibility that the roles of SecD/F and PpiD in arrest cancelation are redundant. Instead, both of them are specifically required for the cancelation of VemP arrest, raising the possibility that they interact with each other.
evidence: Inferred from the genetic complementation experiments showing that overproduction of either factor alone cannot rescue the defect caused by loss of the other.

claim: When pBPA was incorporated into the position of Asp-359 in the P1 head of SecD, its crosslinks with PpiD were detected.
source: We then studied this point by in vivo photo-crosslinking. When pBPA was incorporated into the position of Asp-359 in the P1 head of SecD, its XLs with PpiD were detected (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo photo-crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PpiD resides in close proximity to the mobile P1 head of SecD of the VemP-translocating translocon.
source: Thus, PpiD resides in close proximity to the mobile P1 head of SecD of the VemP-translocating translocon.
evidence: Inferred from the crosslinking of pBPA at position 359 in SecD with PpiD.

claim: Incorporation of pBPA to some VemP residues compromised the translation arrest of VemP.
source: Our systematic pBPA scanning incidentally revealed that incorporation of this amino acid analog to some VemP residues compromised the translation arrest of VemP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by systematic pBPA scanning shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Trp substitutions at several residues destabilized the translation arrest in similar ways to the corresponding pBPA substitutions.
source: We selected several residues among them (shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and replaced them individually with Trp (having a bulky, hydrophobic side chain like pBPA). The Trp substitutions destabilized the translation arrest in similar ways to the corresponding pBPA substitutions.
evidence: Demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The R85W mutation had the strongest effect in destabilizing the translation arrest among the tested mutations.
source: Among them, the R85W mutation had the strongest effect; it decreased the ratio of arrested forms to total VemP to the level comparable with that observed with a previously identified arrest motif mutation, W143A (Mori et al., 2018).
evidence: Demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Several other replacements of Arg-85 by residues of different properties also impaired apparently the translation arrest of VemP.
source: Several other replacements of Arg-85 by residues of different properties also impaired apparently the translation arrest of VemP (Figure 5A).
evidence: Demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The R85W mutation abrogated the arrest-mediated up-regulation of V.secD2.
source: The R85W mutation abrogated the arrest-mediated up-regulation of V.secD2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Arg-85 is crucial for the stable translation arrest of VemP in vivo.
source: These results showed that Arg-85 is crucial for the stable translation arrest of VemP in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the mutagenesis experiments showing that mutations at Arg-85 destabilize the translation arrest and abrogate arrest-mediated regulation.

claim: The R85W mutation did not exert a negative effect on the arrest in the secretion-impaired cell.
source: In the Sec-deficient cells (see Materials and methods), the arrested form of WT VemP was stabilized (Mori et al., 2018), while that of VemP(W143A) was rapidly converted to the full-length form (Figure 5B). In contrast, the R85W mutant did not exert a negative effect on the arrest in the secretion-impaired cell (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments in Sec-deficient cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The R85 mutation did not affect the elongation arrest in the absence of the signal sequence.
source: As another means to render VemP indifferent to secretion, we deleted its signal sequence. The R85 mutation did not affect the elongation arrest in the absence of the signal sequence. By sharp contrast, the W143A mutation abolished the arrest even in the absence of the signal sequence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments using VemP lacking signal sequence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The W143A mutation abolished the arrest even in the absence of the signal sequence.
source: As another means to render VemP indifferent to secretion, we deleted its signal sequence. The R85 mutation did not affect the elongation arrest in the absence of the signal sequence. By sharp contrast, the W143A mutation abolished the arrest even in the absence of the signal sequence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments using VemP lacking signal sequence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The mode of involvement of Arg-85 in the elongation arrest is fundamentally different from that of Trp-143.
source: Thus, the mode of involvement of Arg-85 in the elongation arrest is fundamentally different from that of Trp-143.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of R85 and W143A mutations under secretion-deficient conditions and in the absence of signal sequence.

claim: Arg-85 acts after targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon, probably during its translocation.
source: These data revealed that Arg-85 acts after targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon, probably during its translocation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that R85 mutations only affect arrest under secretion-proficient conditions.

claim: The R85W mutation allows the efficient translocation of VemP even in the absence of PpiD.
source: In the ΔppiD strain, while a significant fraction of the VemP(W143A) was retained in the arrested forms, the VemP(R85W/W143A) double mutant was almost completely translocated to generate the mature (processed) FL form. The results suggest that the R85W mutation allows the efficient translocation of VemP even in the absence of PpiD, indicating that the mutation at Arg-85 reduces PpiD-dependency of the VemP translocation.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mutation at Arg-85 reduces PpiD-dependency of the VemP translocation.
source: In the ΔppiD strain, while a significant fraction of the VemP(W143A) was retained in the arrested forms, the VemP(R85W/W143A) double mutant was almost completely translocated to generate the mature (processed) FL form. The results suggest that the R85W mutation allows the efficient translocation of VemP even in the absence of PpiD, indicating that the mutation at Arg-85 reduces PpiD-dependency of the VemP translocation.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A small but significant amount of the full-length precursor form of VemP(F.S.) was observed in the ΔppiD strain, suggesting the translocation of VemP(F.S.) depends on PpiD.
source: As expected, the VemP(F.S.) derivative no longer underwent the elongation arrest even in the ΔppiD strain. We observed a small but significant amount of the full-length precursor form of VemP(F.S.) in the ΔppiD strain, suggesting the translocation of VemP(F.S.) depends on PpiD.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The additional introduction of the R85W mutation into VemP(F.S.) greatly reduced the amount of the precursor.
source: Interestingly, the additional introduction of the R85W mutation into VemP(F.S.) greatly reduced the amount of the precursor.
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Arg-85 residue somehow retards the translocation of VemP independently of its translation arrest.
source: These results indicate that while the Arg-85 residue somehow retards the translocation of VemP independently of its translation arrest, it is released by the function of PpiD; in other words, Arg-85 imposes PpiD-dependency on the translocation of VemP.
evidence: Inferred from the experiments showing that R85W mutation reduces PpiD-dependency even in the absence of translation arrest.

claim: Arg-85 imposes PpiD-dependency on the translocation of VemP.
source: These results indicate that while the Arg-85 residue somehow retards the translocation of VemP independently of its translation arrest, it is released by the function of PpiD; in other words, Arg-85 imposes PpiD-dependency on the translocation of VemP.
evidence: Inferred from the experiments showing that R85W mutation reduces PpiD-dependency of VemP translocation.

claim: The function of Arg-85 could repress the arrest cancelation of VemP until translocation of VemP proceeds to an appropriate stage, at which PpiD and SecD/F come in to enhance the late stage of translocation.
source: The function of Arg-85 could repress the arrest cancelation of VemP until translocation of VemP proceeds to an appropriate stage, at which PpiD and SecD/F come in to enhance the late stage of translocation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results regarding Arg-85 function.

claim: In the cytosol, SRP recognizes and binds to the signal sequence of VemP and targets the nascent chain to the translocon.
source: (i) In the cytosol, SRP recognizes and binds to the signal sequence of VemP and targets the nascent chain to the translocon. During this co-translational targeting step, the ongoing translation of VemP is subject to elongation arrest.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing SRP interaction with VemP signal sequence and its requirement for membrane targeting.

claim: During the co-translational targeting step, the ongoing translation of VemP is subject to elongation arrest.
source: (i) In the cytosol, SRP recognizes and binds to the signal sequence of VemP and targets the nascent chain to the translocon. During this co-translational targeting step, the ongoing translation of VemP is subject to elongation arrest.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing that VemP undergoes translation arrest.

claim: The signal sequence of VemP is inserted into the lateral gate region while the mature region of VemP is going to span the translocon's polypeptide-conducting channel.
source: (ii) The signal sequence is then inserted into the lateral gate region while the mature region of VemP is going to span the translocon's polypeptide-conducting channel.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing VemP interaction with the translocon.

claim: The early step of translocation is facilitated by the SecA ATPase and accompanied by the signal sequence cleavage.
source: This early step of translocation is facilitated by the SecA ATPase (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and accompanied by the signal sequence cleavage.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing SecA requirement and signal sequence processing.

claim: The inhibition of SecA with NaN3 causes accumulation of the AP-un form of VemP.
source: Therefore, the inhibition of SecA with NaN3 causes accumulation of the AP-un form of VemP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that NaN3 treatment stabilizes the AP-un form.

claim: SecD/F and PpiD interact with VemP and cooperate in canceling the translation arrest of VemP while aiding its further translocation.
source: (iii) SecD/F and PpiD then interact with VemP and cooperate in canceling the translation arrest of VemP while aiding its further translocation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing interactions and functional cooperation between SecD/F and PpiD.

claim: The full-length, mature VemP polypeptide is exported to the periplasm.
source: (iv) Finally, the full-length, mature VemP polypeptide is exported to the periplasm.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing generation of mature full-length VemP.

claim: PpiD and SecD/F seem to cooperate either sequentially or in concert in the arrest cancelation event.
source: In the arrest cancelation event, PpiD and SecD/F seem to cooperate either sequentially or in concert, and our crosslinking results revealed that they physically interact with each other (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic complementation experiments and crosslinking data.

claim: PpiD was a member of the periplasmic chaperone network.
source: PpiD was a member of the periplasmic chaperone network (Dartigalongue and Raina, 1998; Matern et al., 2010), which directly interacts with both SecY/E/G and ribosome-tethered polypeptides (Antonoaea et al., 2008; Sachelaru et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Dartigalongue and Raina, 1998 and Matern et al., 2010.

claim: PpiD directly interacts with both SecY/E/G and ribosome-tethered polypeptides.
source: PpiD was a member of the periplasmic chaperone network (Dartigalongue and Raina, 1998; Matern et al., 2010), which directly interacts with both SecY/E/G and ribosome-tethered polypeptides (Antonoaea et al., 2008; Sachelaru et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Antonoaea et al., 2008 and Sachelaru et al., 2014.

claim: An in vitro study revealed that PpiD stimulates translocation of substrate proteins.
source: Although an in vitro study revealed that PpiD stimulates translocation of substrate proteins (Fürst et al., 2018), the deletion of the ppiD gene caused no detectable defect of outer membrane protein biogenesis (Justice et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Fürst et al., 2018.

claim: The deletion of the ppiD gene caused no detectable defect of outer membrane protein biogenesis.
source: Although an in vitro study revealed that PpiD stimulates translocation of substrate proteins (Fürst et al., 2018), the deletion of the ppiD gene caused no detectable defect of outer membrane protein biogenesis (Justice et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Justice et al., 2005.

claim: PpiD physically contacts SecD as well as the AP-pro form of VemP in vivo.
source: We showed here that PpiD physically contacts SecD as well as the AP-pro form of VemP in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking experiments shown in Figures 1F and 4E.

claim: PpiD has a role in the cancelation of the VemP translation arrest.
source: Furthermore, our genetic and biochemical analyses indicated that PpiD has a role in the cancelation of the VemP translation arrest (Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic and biochemical experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: SecD/F works as a monovalent cation-driven motor that pulls up a translocating polypeptide by undergoing a conformational change of the P1 head.
source: SecD/F works as a monovalent cation-driven motor that pulls up a translocating polypeptide by undergoing a conformational change of the P1 head (Tsukazaki et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Tsukazaki et al., 2011.

claim: The conformational change of the P1 head of SecD/F could generate a pulling force that cancels the VemP elongation arrest.
source: Such an action could generate a pulling force that cancels the VemP elongation arrest.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the known mechanism of SecD/F and its role in VemP arrest cancelation.

claim: PpiD itself would not generate a pulling force against the nascent chain because it is an ATP-independent chaperone.
source: By contrast, PpiD itself would not generate a pulling force against the nascent chain because it is an ATP-independent chaperone (Matern et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the known properties of PpiD as an ATP-independent chaperone, supported by citation to Matern et al., 2010.

claim: PpiD captures a VemP polypeptide emerging from the translocon and then hands it over to the P1 head domain of SecD.
source: It is conceivable that PpiD captures a VemP polypeptide emerging from the translocon and then hand it over to the P1 head domain, which is known as the substrate-binding site of SecD (Furukawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental data showing PpiD and SecD interactions with VemP and each other.

claim: The direct contact between PpiD and SecD facilitates the substrate transfer from PpiD to SecD.
source: Possibly, the direct contact between PpiD and SecD facilitates the substrate transfer from PpiD to SecD.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the crosslinking data showing PpiD-SecD interaction.

claim: The binding of VemP by PpiD helps to prevent the reverse movement of VemP.
source: It is also possible that the binding of VemP by PpiD helps to prevent the reverse movement of VemP.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the role of PpiD in VemP translocation.

claim: Both SecD/F and PpiD are well conserved in enterobacteria including E. coli that possess no VemP protein.
source: Since both SecD/F and PpiD are well conserved in enterobacteria including E. coli that possess no VemP protein, the co-operative function of these proteins could be utilized to stimulate late step translocation of some un-identified secretory proteins in these organisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The co-operative function of SecD/F and PpiD could be utilized to stimulate late step translocation of some un-identified secretory proteins in organisms that lack VemP.
source: Since both SecD/F and PpiD are well conserved in enterobacteria including E. coli that possess no VemP protein, the co-operative function of these proteins could be utilized to stimulate late step translocation of some un-identified secretory proteins in these organisms.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the conservation of SecD/F and PpiD and their cooperative function in VemP translocation.

claim: Arg-85 is highly conserved among the VemP orthologues.
source: Arg-85 is highly conserved among the VemP orthologues (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), pointing to its importance in the VemP function.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Arg-85 does not contribute to the establishment, per se, of the translation-arrested state of VemP, when its secretion is blocked.
source: This residue does not contribute to the establishment, per se, of the translation-arrested state of VemP, when its secretion is blocked (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments in Sec-deficient cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Under the export-proficient conditions, Arg-85 somehow acts to retard the translocation of VemP independently of the translocation arrest of VemP, and consequently increase the PpiD-dependency of the VemP translocation.
source: However, under the export-proficient conditions, Arg-85 somehow acts to retard the translocation of VemP independently of the translocation arrest of VemP, and consequently increase the PpiD-dependency of the VemP translocation (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A region encompassing the Arg-74 to Trp-86 interval interacts with the translocon's components in the arrested state of VemP.
source: Our crosslinking results show that a region encompassing the Arg-74 to Trp-86 interval interacts with the translocon's components in the arrested state of VemP (Figure 6A), indicating that Arg-85 resides in the SecY/E/G-contacting region of the VemP nascent chain (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 1D and summarized in Figure 6A.

claim: Arg-85 resides in the SecY/E/G-contacting region of the VemP nascent chain.
source: Our crosslinking results show that a region encompassing the Arg-74 to Trp-86 interval interacts with the translocon's components in the arrested state of VemP (Figure 6A), indicating that Arg-85 resides in the SecY/E/G-contacting region of the VemP nascent chain (Figure 6A).
evidence: Inferred from the crosslinking data showing that the region containing Arg-85 interacts with the translocon.

claim: Arg-85 interacts with the translocon, which inhibits the forward movement of VemP and stabilizes its elongation-arrested state by antagonizing the translocation force.
source: This spatial arrangement leads us to assume that Arg-85 interacts with the translocon, which inhibits the forward movement of VemP and stabilizes its elongation-arrested state by antagonizing the translocation force that otherwise (when Arg85 is mutated) could lead to a rapid arrest cancelation.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental data showing the role of Arg-85 in stabilizing arrest and its location in the translocon-contacting region.

claim: A force strong enough to overcome the arrest must be applied in the case of wild-type VemP to make it competent for regulation.
source: Thus, a force strong enough to overcome the arrest must be applied in the case of wild-type VemP to make it competent for regulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Arg-85 stabilizes arrest and requires PpiD/SecD/F for arrest cancelation.

claim: The presence of Arg-85 acts as an obstacle for translocation.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that the presence of Arg-85 acts as an obstacle for translocation.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing that Arg-85 retards translocation and increases PpiD-dependency.

claim: The trans-side motor SecD/F with the aide from PpiD would overcome the obstacle posed by Arg-85 and manage to allow translocation and arrest-cancelation to take place with a physiological efficiency.
source: However, the trans-side motor SecD/F with the aide from PpiD would overcome the obstacle and manage to allow translocation and arrest-cancelation to take place with a physiological efficiency.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the experimental data showing the cooperative function of SecD/F and PpiD in overcoming the Arg-85-mediated obstacle.

claim: When Arg-85 is mutated to other amino acid residues, translocation does not meet any obstacle and proceed very rapidly such that we do not see any significant arrest in the Sec-proficient cells.
source: When Arg-85 is mutated to other amino acid residues, translocation does not meet any obstacle and proceed very rapidly such that we do not see any significant arrest in the Sec-proficient cells.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing that Arg-85 mutations destabilize arrest under secretion-proficient conditions.

claim: When the signal sequence of VemP is non-functional or the Sec system is inactivated, the elongation arrest occurs normally and continues stably whether or not Arg85 is mutated.
source: When the signal sequence of VemP is non-functional or the Sec system is inactivated, the elongation arrest occurs normally and continues stably whether or not Arg85 is mutated.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing that Arg-85 mutations do not affect arrest under secretion-deficient conditions.

claim: The VemP arrest cancelation may require a pulling force by the PpiD-SecD/F system in addition to the force generated by SecA, which alone is insufficient.
source: In any case, the VemP arrest cancelation may require a pulling force by the PpiD-SecD/F system in addition to the force generated by SecA, which alone is insufficient.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that both SecA and PpiD/SecD/F are required for efficient arrest cancelation.

claim: Translation and translocation of VemP are tuned to monitor the periplasmic motor activity of the bacterial Sec system.
source: From this line of considerations, we propose that translation and translocation of VemP are tuned to monitor the periplasmic motor activity of the bacterial Sec system.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing that VemP arrest cancelation depends on SecD/F and PpiD, which function at late steps of translocation.

claim: Monitoring substrates employ different force-generation mechanisms to enable real-time monitoring of local events of polypeptide translocation, which is superimposed with temporal elements of translation.
source: Remarkably, monitoring substrates employ different force-generation mechanisms to enable real-time monitoring of local events of polypeptide translocation, which is superimposed with temporal elements of translation.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the comparison of different monitoring substrates including VemP, SecM, and MifM.

claim: SecM also possesses a cis-element that is located outside the ribosome in the arrested translation complex and required for the efficient arrest cancelation.
source: Interestingly, SecM also possesses a cis-element that is located outside the ribosome in the arrested translation complex and required for the efficient arrest cancelation (Ito et al., 2018; Nakamori et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Ito et al., 2018 and Nakamori et al., 2014.

claim: The regulatory target of SecM is SecA.
source: The regulatory target of SecM is SecA (Nakatogawa and Ito, 2001), and its arrest is canceled at an early stage of translocation, before the cleavage of the signal sequence (Mori et al., 2018; Nakatogawa and Ito, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Nakatogawa and Ito, 2001 and Mori et al., 2018.

claim: The arrest of SecM is canceled at an early stage of translocation, before the cleavage of the signal sequence.
source: The regulatory target of SecM is SecA (Nakatogawa and Ito, 2001), and its arrest is canceled at an early stage of translocation, before the cleavage of the signal sequence (Mori et al., 2018; Nakatogawa and Ito, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Mori et al., 2018 and Nakatogawa and Ito, 2001.

claim: SecM may monitor the SecA-stimulated early translocation event via its cis-element.
source: SecM may monitor the SecA-stimulated early translocation event via its cis-element.
evidence: This is inferred from the known properties of SecM and its cis-element.

claim: A role of the cis-element in SecM should be different with that of Arg-85 in VemP.
source: Thus, a role of the cis-element in SecM should be different with that of Arg-85 in VemP.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of SecM and VemP mechanisms.
